titleEn: Ground-Level Fall in an 82-Year-Old - Hip Fracture on Anticoagulants

patient.name: Margaret Ellis
patient.affectEn: alert, apologetic and embarrassed about the fuss; in obvious pain whenever she or her leg is moved; lying on her right side on the hallway carpet
patient.speechEn: clear full sentences, polite and cooperative; wears a hearing aid in her left ear and wants things explained before they are done; answers exactly what she is asked

scene.settingEn: Tidy one-bedroom suite on the fourth floor of a seniors' independent living building on Bernard Avenue in Kelowna, 1840 hrs. Warm, dry summer evening, 26 degrees C; the suite itself is a comfortable room temperature with good lighting. The building has an elevator; the suite opens onto a narrow hallway. A loose scatter rug is rucked up at the edge of the hallway; her walker stands three metres away by the kitchen. One patient, lying on her right side on the carpeted hallway floor between the bathroom and the bedroom, fully dressed. Her daughter is with her, calm, and has not moved her. Kelowna General Hospital is 12 minutes away.
hazardsEn: no significant hazards; the rucked-up scatter rug at the edge of the hallway (the likely trip hazard)
narrow hallway and a fourth-floor suite - plan the route out to the elevator before moving her

bystanders.knowsEn: She called 911 and has not moved her mother. Her mother takes a blood thinner, apixaban - the last dose was this morning - plus metoprolol, ramipril, calcium and vitamin D; she can bring the medication list. Her mother has atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure and osteoporosis and broke her wrist once before. Her mother uses a walker outdoors but not indoors. She knows nothing about the fall beyond what her mother says, and will hand over her contact information and her mother's glasses if asked.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: extra padding, pillows and rolled blankets
stair chair (not needed - there is an elevator)
oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
drug kit: oral acetaminophen, oral ibuprofen, Entonox
PCP only: IV start kit, IV acetaminophen, ondansetron

dispatchEn: 1840 hrs. Code 2 to a seniors' independent living apartment on Bernard Avenue in Kelowna. An 82-year-old woman has fallen in her suite and cannot get up. Her daughter is with her and called 911. Warm, dry summer evening, 26 degrees C. No fire or police response. Kelowna General Hospital is 12 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: the patient is conscious and talking, complaining of right hip pain, and has been on the floor for about 20 minutes. The daughter says her mother takes a blood thinner. The building has an elevator and the suite is on the fourth floor with a narrow hallway.
arrivalEn: The elevator takes you to the fourth floor and the daughter lets you into a tidy one-bedroom suite. Good lighting, comfortable room temperature, no hazards apart from a loose scatter rug rucked up at the edge of the hallway. A walker stands about three metres away by the kitchen. One patient, lying on her right side on the carpeted hallway floor between the bathroom and the bedroom, fully dressed. The daughter is calm and tells you she has not moved her mother.
firstLookEn: An elderly woman lying on her right side on the hallway carpet, awake and watching you, fully dressed. She is in obvious pain. Her right leg is visibly shortened and rotated outward. No blood on the floor.

primary.locEn: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time and event; GCS 15. She remembers the whole fall. (If asked what happened: she caught her foot on the rug, went straight down on her right side, never hit her head and never blacked out.)
primary.airwayEn: Clear. She is speaking in full sentences.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 18, regular and unlaboured. Good air entry bilaterally.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 92, irregularly irregular, good volume. (If asked whether that is normal for her: she has atrial fibrillation and it is always irregular.) No pallor, no external hemorrhage.
primary.rbsEn: Head and neck: no injury, no midline cervical tenderness. Chest and abdomen: non-tender. Pelvis: gentle palpation only - the right groin is exquisitely tender; if the candidate springs, rocks or compresses the pelvis, record pelvis-sprung and give no further pelvic finding. Right hip and groin exquisitely tender; right leg shortened by about 3 cm and externally rotated. Left leg normal. Arms: no deformity. No external hemorrhage. Both feet warm with strong pedal pulses, normal sensation and normal toe movement. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: warm, dry and pink.

history.ccEn: It's my right hip. Well, the groin really. I fell and I can't get up.

opqrst.oEn: I caught my foot on that rug and went straight down on my right side. About 20 minutes ago.
opqrst.pEn: Any movement at all makes it much worse. Nothing makes it better. I haven't tried to stand up.
opqrst.qEn: Sharp when anything moves. When I lie still it's a deep ache.
opqrst.rEn: It goes down towards my knee.
opqrst.sEn: Oh, it's bad. An 8 out of 10.
opqrst.tEn: Ever since I fell, about 20 minutes. It hasn't eased at all.

history.painScoreEn: 8 out of 10 in the right groin (sharp with any movement, a deep ache at rest). After acetaminophen and Entonox, once she is packaged: 4 out of 10 at rest.

sample.sEn: Just the pain in my hip and groin. (Only if asked specifically: no dizziness, no palpitations, no chest pain and no shortness of breath before the fall, and I didn't faint.)
sample.mEn: Apixaban - that's my blood thinner, I took it this morning. Metoprolol, ramipril, and calcium and vitamin D.
sample.pEn: Atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure and osteoporosis. I broke my wrist once before. I've had cataract surgery on both eyes.
sample.lEn: Soup and tea at half past five.
sample.eEn: I caught my foot on that rug and tripped - I went straight down on my right side. I didn't hit my head and I didn't black out; I remember all of it. (Only if asked: I wasn't dizzy, my heart wasn't racing, no chest pain, I wasn't short of breath, and I didn't faint first.)

fe.generalEn: I've been more tired lately. My appetite is good and I haven't lost weight. I use the walker outdoors but not inside.
fe.cnsEn: No dizziness, no headache, I'm not confused. I've never had a stroke. No numbness anywhere.
fe.respiratoryEn: No cough. I'm not short of breath.
fe.cardiovascularEn: I have atrial fibrillation. No chest pain. My ankles swell up sometimes.
fe.giGuEn: No tummy pain, no vomiting. No blood in my stool or my urine. I haven't passed water since I fell.
fe.integumentaryEn: My skin is thin and tears easily. There's a big bruise coming up on my right hip.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Just the right hip, it's very sore. No other joints hurt. I broke my wrist once before.
fe.eentEn: I've had cataract surgery on both eyes. I wear a hearing aid in my left ear.

findings.headNeckEn: No injury to the head or neck, no bruising behind the ears, no midline cervical tenderness on gentle palpation.
findings.chestLungsEn: No tenderness. Equal air entry at all six sites.
findings.backEn: Inspected during the scoop transfer: no tenderness; an old kyphosis - the voids under her head and shoulders need padding rather than forcing her flat.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Right leg shortened by about 3 cm and externally rotated, with a large early bruise over the right hip and exquisite groin tenderness. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses strong bilaterally; sensation and toe movement normal bilaterally. Left leg entirely normal.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: A small skin tear on the right forearm from the fall; CSM intact in both arms.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline, on scene (required before acetaminophen and Entonox)

in the ambulance after analgesia and packaging (after acetaminophen or Entonox, and once loaded or 20 minutes into the call); pain now 4/10 at rest; right pedal pulses still strong with normal sensation and toe movement. Without analgesia set 1 values persist.

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: She cries out as she is moved and grips your arm - the pain in her groin is much worse with the movement.
As the binder is tightened she cries out - the pain in her right hip is much worse.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan equipment for a fourth-floor extrication down a narrow hallway: scoop stretcher, extra padding and pillows, blankets, stair chair if needed, and the drug kit
triggers: plan the extrication from the fourth floor

expected.actionEn: Anticipate the two geriatric questions this call will turn on: why did she fall, and what does the anticoagulant change about her risk of bleeding
triggers: find out what caused the fall

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (none significant, note the rucked scatter rug as the likely trip hazard), environment, MOI (fall from standing height onto carpet), people (one patient plus a calm daughter) and resources
triggers: the rug is the trip hazard
mechanism is a fall from standing

expected.actionEn: Don gloves; introduce yourself to the patient by name, get down to her eye level and ask permission before touching her
triggers: is it okay if I touch you

expected.actionEn: First look: elderly woman lying on her side, alert and oriented, in obvious pain, with the right leg visibly shortened and rotated outward; no blood on the floor
triggers: she looks to be in pain

expected.actionEn: Assess LOC / AVPU: alert and oriented, GCS 15 - and say so, because an elderly patient's baseline mental status matters to the receiving team
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Apply the NEXUS criteria out loud and correctly conclude spinal motion restriction is NOT indicated: no midline tenderness, no focal deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no distracting injury above the pelvis - but re-check if she reports any neck pain during movement
Assess the airway - patent, speaking in full sentences
Assess breathing with auscultation of both lung fields
Assess circulation: note the irregularly irregular pulse and ask whether that is normal for her, and look for the pallor or tachycardia that would suggest occult bleeding in an anticoagulated patient
Rapid body survey head to toe with a gentle approach; do NOT spring or rock the pelvis, and check distal pulses, sensation and movement in both feet
triggers: not going to spring the pelvis

expected.actionEn: Note the skin as warm, dry and pink - normal perfusion
triggers: skin is warm dry and pink

expected.actionEn: Oxygen is not indicated at SpO2 96% with normal work of breathing - state that and do not apply it reflexively
Position of comfort with the injured limb supported in the position found, using rolled blankets and pillows to eliminate motion at the hip
triggers: support the leg where it is

expected.actionEn: Correctly categorize as non-RTC and state the reason: an isolated hip injury with intact neurovascular status distal to the injury
State the findings that would upgrade her to RTC: an absent or weakening pedal pulse, new sensory or motor loss, or developing shock
triggers: if she loses a pedal pulse

expected.actionEn: Ready for transport within 30 minutes, having planned the route out of a fourth-floor suite through a narrow hallway before the patient is moved
triggers: plan the route to the elevator

expected.actionEn: Establish the chief complaint: right hip pain and inability to stand after a fall

HxC/C with OPQRRRST plus the critical fall questions, and specifically hunt for a medical cause: dizziness, palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, syncope, new medications, or a fall that was witnessed as a collapse rather than a trip
Pain score before and after any analgesia and before and after moving her
Past medical history, including previous fractures and osteoporosis
Medications - identify apixaban as an anticoagulant and recognize both that it raises her bleeding risk and that it contraindicates ibuprofen
Allergies
Last oral intake - relevant because she is heading for surgery
GCS with all three components
Blood pressure by auscultation; compare it with her usual readings and be alert that a normal or high pressure does not exclude bleeding in an older patient on antihypertensives
Pulse - describe the irregularly irregular rhythm and confirm it is her known atrial fibrillation
Respiratory rate, depth and character
Skin assessed hands-on
Pupils
SpO2
Blood glucose - justified in an older adult who has fallen, to rule out hypoglycaemia as the cause
Temperature - a long lie on the floor and possible infection as a fall precipitant both justify it
FE - General health (frailty, mobility aids and recent decline are the key geriatric threads)
FE - CNS (ruling out a neurological cause for the fall)
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular (atrial fibrillation and a possible arrhythmic cause for the fall)
FE - GI/GU (occult bleeding on an anticoagulant, and urinary retention after a long lie)
FE - Integumentary (fragile skin and pressure areas after 20 minutes on the floor)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (hearing aid and vision affect how you communicate with her)
Head and neck examined gently, including behind the ears, in an anticoagulated patient who might have struck her head without realizing it
Chest examined with six-site auscultation
Abdomen examined - occult retroperitoneal bleeding is a real risk on an anticoagulant
Back examined during the scoop transfer, with the kyphosis padded rather than forced flat
Upper extremities including the skin tear and CSM
Lower extremities with the shortening and rotation measured and both pedal pulses, sensation and movement documented before and after every move
Stabilize the injured limb where it lies using helpers, rolled blankets and a pillow between the legs, then move her with a scoop onto a firm padded surface and secure her to eliminate hip movement
triggers: secure her to eliminate hip movement

expected.actionEn: Administer acetaminophen 500-1,000 mg PO before moving her, after confirming she has taken none in the past 4 hours and has no liver disease
triggers: any Tylenol in the last 4 hours

expected.actionEn: Offer self-administered Entonox before the move, after baseline vitals with SpO2 and after ruling out the contraindications - she is alert, can comply, and the suite can be ventilated
Explicitly withhold ibuprofen and state the reason: she is on the anticoagulant apixaban, which is a listed contraindication
Do NOT apply a pelvic binder; verbalize that a neck-of-femur fracture and a fall from standing height are both contraindications to binding
triggers: hip fracture is a contraindication to binding

expected.actionEn: Geriatric care details: pad the voids for the kyphosis and heels, keep her warm, keep her glasses and hearing aid with her, explain each step before you do it, and bring her medication list and the daughter's contact information
Reassess ABCs and interventions after each of the four moves
Recheck distal pulses, sensation and movement in the injured leg after every move and document each check
Second full set of vitals within 15 minutes for a non-priority patient
Re-score the pain after analgesia and after the move, and document the response
Notification appropriate to a non-priority patient, flagging the anticoagulant
Complete hand-off including analgesia given, the response to it, and serial neurovascular checks
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes, documenting why ibuprofen was withheld

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate (or a helper on the candidate's instruction) actually applies a pelvic binder or triangular bandages around the pelvis. Saying a binder is contraindicated or not needed, strapping her body to the scoop or spinal device, and a pillow with ties between the legs are NOT this event.

candidate takes manual c-spine control, applies a hard collar or head blocks, or straps her head down for spinal motion restriction. Placing her on a padded scoop or spinal device and securing her body to eliminate movement at the HIP is correct and is NOT this event.
candidate springs, rocks or compresses the pelvis (pushes the iliac crests together or apart); gentle palpation is NOT this event
candidate pulls the shortened, externally rotated right leg straight, realigns it, or applies traction or a traction splint to it, instead of supporting it in the position found
candidate asks or lets the patient sit up, stand, take weight on the leg or walk at any point (e.g. to get to the cot)

candidate administers a medication without having asked about or examined for that medication's contraindications at any earlier point in the call (Entonox: altered LOC, ability to comply, chest injury / pneumothorax, a room that can be ventilated; acetaminophen: liver disease, acetaminophen in the past 4 hours). The standard history (medical history, medications, allergies) counts when it was done earlier.
candidate gives acetaminophen at a dose other than 500 - 1,000 mg PO (a PCP may instead give 1,000 mg IV over 15 minutes), or gives it IV at EMR level
candidate starts Entonox without stating that the cylinder is inverted (3 times) before use
candidate applies supplemental oxygen (non-rebreather or nasal cannula) at SpO2 96% with normal work of breathing, with no titration rationale; Entonox itself is NOT this event

candidate asks about a medical cause for the fall: dizziness or light-headedness, palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting or blacking out beforehand, or directly asks why she fell / whether she tripped or collapsed (good act; also detected from the candidate's words)

drugs.doseEn: inhalation, self-administered; invert the cylinder 3 times before use; give BEFORE she is moved or the limb is manipulated, after the primary survey, a pain assessment, baseline vitals with SpO2 and the contraindication screen
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin in the last 5 minutes (none apply to her)
drugs.cautionsEn: shock; abdominal distention; depressant drugs; COPD; facial injuries

drugs.doseEn: 500 - 1,000 mg PO, single dose on this call, before she is moved (PCP alternative: 1,000 mg IV over 15 minutes for a patient 50 kg or more)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity; severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease; acetaminophen within the past 4 hours; suspected overdose (none apply to her)

drugs.doseEn: 300-400 mg PO - WITHHELD in this scenario: she takes apixaban, and anticoagulants are a listed contraindication
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity to ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; active GI hemorrhage or ulcers; pregnancy; anticoagulants (APPLIES - apixaban)

drugs.doseEn: 4 mg PO (adult dose), PCP only, for moderate to severe nausea - e.g. if Entonox makes her nauseated (she is not nauseated in this script)

notificationFacts.moi: tripped on a scatter rug at about 1820 and fell from standing height onto her right side on carpet; no head strike, no loss of consciousness
notificationFacts.hxcc: on the floor about 20 minutes; right groin pain 8/10, sharp with movement, radiating to the knee; a mechanical trip with no dizziness, palpitations, chest pain or shortness of breath beforehand
notificationFacts.vitals: GCS 15, BP 148/86, pulse 92 irregularly irregular (known atrial fibrillation), resp 18, SpO2 96% on room air; latest BP 138/80, pulse 88, resp 16, SpO2 97%, pain 4/10
notificationFacts.treatments: limb supported in the position found, acetaminophen PO and self-administered Entonox before the move, scoop transfer to a padded firm surface with the hip immobilized; ibuprofen withheld (apixaban); no pelvic binder; ETA 12 minutes
notificationFacts.findings: right leg shortened about 3 cm and externally rotated with intact distal pulses, sensation and movement; takes apixaban (anticoagulant) - flagged

handoffFacts.cc: right groin and hip pain, unable to stand after a fall
handoffFacts.moi: tripped on a scatter rug at approximately 1820 and fell from standing height onto her right side on carpet; no head strike, no loss of consciousness
handoffFacts.hxcc: clear that she tripped rather than collapsed - no dizziness, palpitations, chest pain or shortness of breath beforehand; on the floor about 20 minutes; groin pain initially 8/10, sharp with movement, radiating to the knee, 4/10 at rest after analgesia
handoffFacts.initialVitals: GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6), BP 148/86, pulse 92 irregularly irregular (known atrial fibrillation), resp 18 regular unlaboured, skin warm dry pink, pupils equal and reactive, SpO2 96% on room air, BGL 6.2 mmol/L, temperature 36.8 C
handoffFacts.finalVitals: GCS 15, BP 138/80, pulse 88 irregularly irregular, resp 16 regular, skin warm dry pink, pupils equal and reactive, SpO2 97% on room air, pain 4/10 at rest; right pedal pulses strong with normal sensation and toe movement
handoffFacts.pmhx: atrial fibrillation, hypertension, osteoporosis with a previous wrist fracture, bilateral cataract surgery
handoffFacts.meds: apixaban (anticoagulant - last dose this morning, flagged), metoprolol, ramipril, calcium, vitamin D
handoffFacts.treatments: NEXUS applied and spinal motion restriction not applied; limb supported in the position found with rolled blankets and a pillow between the legs; acetaminophen PO before movement; self-administered Entonox before the move; scoop transfer onto a padded firm surface with the hip immobilized and the voids padded for her kyphosis; ibuprofen withheld because of the apixaban; no pelvic binder (neck-of-femur fracture from a standing-height fall); kept warm, glasses and hearing aid kept with her; last oral intake soup and tea at 1730
handoffFacts.findings: right leg shortened about 3 cm and externally rotated with an early large hip bruise and exquisite groin tenderness; distal pulses, sensation and toe movement intact bilaterally at every check; no head or neck injury, no midline cervical tenderness; small right forearm skin tear; BGL 6.2 and temperature 36.8 - no hypoglycaemic or febrile cause for the fall

pcrFacts.hxcc: Tripped on a scatter rug at 1820, fell from standing height onto the right side on carpet, on the floor about 20 minutes; no head strike, no LOC, no preceding dizziness, palpitations, chest pain or shortness of breath; groin pain 8/10 sharp on movement, radiating to the knee, reduced to 4/10 after analgesia

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You examined her legs and her hips during your rapid body survey - what did you find?

trackNotes.emrEn: Everything this call needs is inside EMR scope: NEXUS applied and spinal motion restriction correctly withheld, the limb supported in the position found with blankets and pillows, a scoop transfer onto a padded firm surface with the hip immobilized, warmth, pressure-area padding for fragile skin, acetaminophen 500-1,000 mg PO, and self-administered Entonox before the move. The two EMR judgement calls that carry the marks are withholding ibuprofen because of the apixaban, and withholding the pelvic binder because a neck-of-femur fracture from a standing-height fall is a contraindication to binding. Both must be verbalized, not silently skipped. IV analgesia and antiemetics are out of scope.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry, vascular access if the transport is long or the pain is severe, IV acetaminophen 1,000 mg over 15 minutes for a patient 50 kg or more as an alternative to oral, and ondansetron 4 mg PO (the guideline adult dose) if Entonox makes her nauseated. PCP should also consider whether an occult retroperitoneal or intracranial bleed is developing on the anticoagulant and reassess the abdomen and LOC serially. Ibuprofen stays withheld (apixaban).

sourcePages: Scenario etr-02 (data/practical/emr-trauma-1.json): dispatch, scene, primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions (EMR scope, analgesia before movement, ibuprofen contraindication, binder trap), ongoing, handoff, critical pitfalls. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (none met); p.11 primary survey interventions (stabilizing fractures; oxygen indications); p.12 critical history questions for a fall (cause of fall); p.21 Musculoskeletal Injuries (stabilize the hip, check distal pulses throughout, analgesia prior to movement in stable appropriate patients); p.22 Hip Dislocation/Fracture (isolated hip fracture is rapid transport only with neuro or vascular impairment; support with helpers, rolled blankets and ties; firm blanketed stretcher or spinal device secured to eliminate hip motion; regular distal checks; pain management); p.24 Pelvis binding (contraindications: neck-of-femur fractures, falls from standing height); p.25 Spinal Management (NEXUS / Canadian C-Spine); p.48 Nausea - Vomiting PCP; p.58-59 Acetaminophen (500 - 1,000 mg PO; IV 1000 mg over 15 minutes for 50 kg or more; contraindications); p.60 Aspirin (ASA is the only medication that vitals are not required for); p.65 Entonox (prerequisites: primary survey, pain investigated, baseline vitals with SpO2, contraindications ruled out; invert cylinder 3 times); p.68 Ibuprofen (contraindicated with anticoagulants); p.75 Ondansetron (adult dose 4 mg PO). EMALB Practical Grading Criteria p.35 (non-priority vitals: 17-18 minutes between sets = moderate delay, > 19 minutes = major) and Appendix A (Pain Management).
